slides.headline: September 22, 1991: India lost the widow who broke a taboo and reshaped who could act on screen.
Durga Khote died on September 22, 1991, at age 86
slides.body: Born into a respectable, English-educated family in 1905, she was widowed at 26 with two young sons to raise alone. In 1931 she took a minor role in the silent film Farebi Jaal - a profession her own class considered disreputable for a woman of her background.

slides.headline: A 50-year, 200-film career - and permission for respectable women to follow her.
slides.body: She went on to act in roughly 200 films and countless stage productions across five decades, most famously as Jodhabai in Mughal-e-Azam (1960), earning a Filmfare nomination. In 2000, India Today named her among the '100 People Who Shaped India.' In 1983 she received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, Indian cinema's highest honor, for lifetime contribution.

slides.eyebrow: Why it matters for Viksit Bharat 2047
slides.headline: Necessity broke the taboo. Talent kept the door open.
slides.body: A Viksit Bharat by 2047 needs every field open on merit, not birth or circumstance. Durga Khote didn't wait for acting to become respectable - she walked in out of necessity and made it respectable by being undeniably good at it.

sources.text: The Quint - Durga Khote: The First Woman, Man Enough to Play a Woman On-Screen
